experiences.title: Graphing functions
experiences.summary: Change a, b and c and watch a line, a parabola or a wave move.
experiences.assumptions: Values are computed exactly; the graph shows x from -10 to 10.

guide.explore: Drag the sliders and watch the curve. What does each letter do?
guide.learn: A function turns each x into one y. In y = a·x + b, a is the slope (how steep) and b is where the line crosses the y-axis. In a parabola, the sign of a decides whether it opens up or down.
steps: Pick the line. Set b to 0 and change a. What happens when a is negative?
Pick the parabola. Find values where it never crosses the x-axis.
Pick the wave. Change b and count how many waves fit between -10 and 10.
guide.advanced: For a parabola the turning point is at x = -b / (2a), and the roots come from the quadratic formula x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a). The wave's period is 2π / |b|.

suggestions: What does a do to the graph?
Why does the parabola have no roots sometimes?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: 3D solids: volume and surface area
experiences.summary: Turn a cube, cylinder, cone or sphere in 3D and see its volume and surface area change.
experiences.assumptions: Exact formulas. The 3D view is a drawing to help you see the shape.

guide.explore: Drag the shape to turn it. Make it taller, then wider. Which change makes the volume grow faster?
guide.learn: Volume is how much space a solid fills, in cubic centimetres. Surface area is the total area of its outside, in square centimetres. A cone holds exactly one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.
steps: Make a cylinder with radius 3 and height 6. Note its volume.
Switch to a cone with the same numbers. Compare the volumes.
Double the radius of a sphere. How many times bigger is the volume?
guide.advanced: Cuboid V = lwh. Cylinder V = πr²h, A = 2πr² + 2πrh. Cone V = πr²h/3, A = πr² + πr√(r² + h²). Sphere V = 4πr³/3, A = 4πr².

suggestions: Why is a cone one third of a cylinder?
What happens to volume when I double the radius?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Projectile motion
experiences.summary: Launch a ball at any speed and angle, on Earth, the Moon or Mars, and measure how far it goes.
experiences.assumptions: No air resistance, flat ground, constant gravity. Real balls fall short of these numbers.

guide.explore: Press Play. Then change the angle and play again. Which angle sends the ball furthest?
guide.learn: Once the ball leaves, gravity is the only force (we ignore air). It pulls the ball down at a steady rate, while the sideways speed stays the same. That is why the path is a curve called a parabola.
steps: Keep the speed at 15 m/s. Try 30°, 45° and 60°. Which goes furthest?
Try 30° and 60°. What do you notice about the distance?
Switch to the Moon. How much further does the same throw go?
guide.advanced: With launch height h: x(t) = v·cosθ·t, y(t) = h + v·sinθ·t − g·t²/2. Time of flight t = (v·sinθ + √((v·sinθ)² + 2gh)) / g. On flat ground (h = 0) the range is v²·sin2θ / g, largest at 45°.

suggestions: Why does 45° go furthest?
Why do 30° and 60° land in the same place?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Gas in a box
experiences.summary: Heat, squeeze or add gas to a box and watch the pressure change.
experiences.assumptions: Ideal gas law. The moving particles are an illustration: their speed follows the temperature, but they are not counted to get the pressure.

guide.explore: Make the box smaller. Then make the gas hotter. What happens to the pressure each time?
guide.learn: Gas particles fly around and hit the walls. Pressure is how hard and how often they hit. Hotter particles move faster, and a smaller box means more hits, so both raise the pressure.
steps: Halve the volume from 40 L to 20 L. What happens to the pressure?
Put the volume back. Double the temperature from 200 K to 400 K.
Double the amount of gas. Which other change had the same effect?
guide.advanced: PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). With P in kPa and V in litres, P = nRT / V. Temperature must be in kelvin: K = °C + 273.15.

suggestions: Why does a smaller box raise the pressure?
Why must temperature be in kelvin?
experiences.safety: Never heat a sealed container in real life: the pressure can make it burst.
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Predators and prey
experiences.summary: Rabbits and foxes rise and fall together. Change how fast they breed and hunt.
experiences.assumptions: A simple model (Lotka-Volterra): prey have unlimited food, predators eat only this prey. Real populations are messier.

guide.explore: Press Play and watch both lines. Which one peaks first, rabbits or foxes?
guide.learn: More rabbits feed more foxes, so foxes increase. More foxes eat more rabbits, so rabbits fall. Then foxes starve and fall too, and the cycle starts again.
steps: Press Play. Does the fox peak come before or after the rabbit peak?
Raise the fox death rate. What happens to the cycles?
Set the start values to the balance point. What do the lines do?
guide.advanced: dR/dt = αR − βRF and dF/dt = δRF − γF. The balance point is R = γ/δ, F = α/β. The model is solved step by step with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method.

suggestions: Why do the fox numbers peak after the rabbits?
What would happen with no foxes at all?
experiences.review: Model checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Ohm's law circuit
experiences.summary: A battery and two resistors in series or parallel. Watch the current and the power change.
experiences.assumptions: Ideal battery and wires with no resistance. The moving dots show the direction of conventional current; their speed is illustrative.

guide.explore: Raise the battery voltage, then raise a resistor. What happens to the current?
guide.learn: Voltage pushes charge around the circuit. Resistance slows it. Ohm's law links them: current = voltage ÷ resistance. In series the resistances add up; in parallel the current has two paths, so the total resistance goes down.
steps: With one resistor of 100 Ω, double the voltage. What happens to the current?
Switch to series. Is the total resistance bigger or smaller than each resistor?
Switch to parallel with two equal resistors. What is the total resistance now?
guide.advanced: I = V / R. Series: R = R1 + R2. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Power P = V·I = I²R.

suggestions: Why does parallel lower the total resistance?
What does a resistor do in a real circuit?
experiences.safety: Mains electricity is dangerous. Only build real circuits with small batteries and an adult's help.
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Piano and intervals
experiences.summary: Play a piano with your mouse or keyboard. See each note's name and frequency, and the interval between two notes.
experiences.assumptions: Equal temperament tuning with A4 = 440 Hz. The sound is made by your browser, not recorded.

guide.explore: Play some keys. Use the letters A S D F G H J K on a computer keyboard too.
guide.learn: Each key is a note. Going up one key is a semitone. Going up 12 keys is an octave, and the frequency doubles. An interval is the distance between two notes.
steps: Play A, then the A one octave up. Compare their frequencies.
Play C then G. Which interval is it?
Change the sound. Does the frequency change, or only how it sounds?
guide.advanced: f = 440 × 2^((n − 69) / 12), where n is the MIDI note number (A4 = 69). A perfect fifth is 7 semitones, a ratio close to 3:2.

suggestions: Why does an octave sound like the same note?
What makes a fifth sound good?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a music teacher.

experiences.title: Moon phases
experiences.summary: Move the Moon around the Earth and see why it looks like a crescent, a half or a full circle.
experiences.assumptions: A simplified model: a circular orbit seen from above the North Pole, sizes and distances not to scale. The cycle is 29.5 days.

guide.explore: Press Play and watch the Moon go round. Look at the small picture: that is what we see from Earth.
guide.learn: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon goes round the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. That is a phase.
steps: Find the new moon. Where is the Moon compared with the Sun?
Move to day 7 or 8. Why is it called a quarter moon when we see half?
How many days from one full moon to the next?
guide.advanced: The lit fraction we see is (1 − cos φ) / 2, where φ is the Moon's angle from new moon. The 29.5-day cycle (synodic month) is longer than one orbit (27.3 days) because the Earth also moves round the Sun.

suggestions: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
Why is a half moon called a quarter?
experiences.review: Geometry checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Earthquake waves: how far away?
experiences.summary: P waves arrive first, S waves later. Use the gap between them to find how far away an earthquake was.
experiences.assumptions: Constant wave speeds through rock (real speeds change with depth). The seismogram shape is an illustration; the arrival times are calculated.

guide.explore: Press Play and watch the seismograph. Then move the earthquake further away. What happens to the gap?
guide.learn: An earthquake sends out two main waves. P waves are faster and arrive first. S waves are slower. The further away the earthquake, the bigger the gap between them.
steps: Note the gap at 100 km and at 200 km. How are they related?
If the gap is 40 seconds, about how far away was the earthquake?
Why do scientists need three stations to find the exact place?
guide.advanced: gap = d/vS − d/vP, so d = gap ÷ (1/vS − 1/vP). With 6 and 3.5 km/s, each second of gap is about 8.4 km.

suggestions: Why are P waves faster than S waves?
How do three stations find an earthquake?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Two-joint robot arm
experiences.summary: Turn the shoulder and elbow of a robot arm and see where its hand ends up.
experiences.assumptions: A flat two-joint arm with rigid links and no weight.

guide.explore: Move the two angles. Can you touch the ground on the far right?
guide.learn: A robot works out where its hand is from its joint angles and the length of each part. This is called forward kinematics.
steps: Set the elbow to 0. What is the reach?
Keep the shoulder still and move the elbow. What shape does the hand draw?
Find two different pairs of angles that put the hand in the same place.
guide.advanced: x = L1·cos θ1 + L2·cos(θ1 + θ2), y = L1·sin θ1 + L2·sin(θ1 + θ2). Working backwards from a target (inverse kinematics) usually has two answers: elbow up and elbow down.

suggestions: Why can two different angle pairs reach the same point?
How does a real robot know its joint angles?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Gear trains
experiences.summary: Change the teeth on two gears and see how speed, turning force and direction change.
experiences.assumptions: Ideal gears with no friction or slipping.

guide.explore: Press Play. Make the driven gear bigger. Does it turn faster or slower?
guide.learn: Meshed gears share the same teeth per second. A big gear driven by a small one turns slower but with more force. Two meshed gears always turn in opposite directions.
steps: Set 12 and 36 teeth. How many times does the small gear turn for one turn of the big one?
Swap the numbers. What happens to the speed?
Which setting would help a bicycle climb a hill?
guide.advanced: Ratio = driven teeth : driving teeth. Output speed = input speed × driving teeth ÷ driven teeth. Ideal torque is multiplied by the same ratio, so power stays the same.

suggestions: Why do bicycles have different gears?
Why do meshed gears turn opposite ways?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Sorting algorithms
experiences.summary: Watch bubble, insertion and selection sort put bars in order, and count every comparison and swap.
experiences.assumptions: Each step is one comparison. The counts are exact for this list.

guide.explore: Press Play and watch the bars. Then try another algorithm on the same number of bars.
guide.learn: An algorithm is a set of exact steps. Sorting algorithms compare two items at a time and decide whether to swap them. Some need far more comparisons than others.
steps: Sort 10 bars with each algorithm. Which needs the fewest swaps?
Double the number of bars. Roughly how many more comparisons does bubble sort need?
Use Step to go one comparison at a time. Explain what insertion sort is doing.
guide.advanced: All three take about n²/2 comparisons in the worst case (O(n²)). Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps. Faster algorithms such as merge sort need about n·log₂n comparisons.

suggestions: Why is bubble sort called bubble sort?
Which algorithm would you use for a big list?
experiences.review: Algorithms checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Latitude, longitude and distance
experiences.summary: Place two points on a globe. See the shortest distance between them and the difference in sun time.
experiences.assumptions: Earth treated as a sphere with radius 6,371 km. Sun time differs from clock time zones, which follow borders.

guide.explore: Point A starts near Kumasi, Ghana and point B near London. Drag the globe to turn it, then move the points.
guide.learn: Latitude says how far north or south of the equator a place is. Longitude says how far east or west of the prime meridian it is. Together they give every place an address.
steps: Move both points onto the equator, 90° of longitude apart. How far apart are they?
Move point B to the North Pole. What happens to the distance as you change B's longitude?
Every 15° of longitude is how many hours of sun time?
guide.advanced: Great-circle distance uses the haversine formula: a = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ1 · cos φ2 · sin²(Δλ/2), d = 2R · atan2(√a, √(1 − a)). Sun time difference = Δλ / 15 hours.

suggestions: Why is the shortest route on a globe curved on a flat map?
Why are time zones not straight lines?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.

experiences.title: Earth's energy balance
experiences.summary: Change sunlight, ice cover and greenhouse gases, and see the planet's average temperature respond.
experiences.assumptions: A one-number climate model: the whole planet has one average temperature and reaches balance instantly. Real climate has oceans, clouds and feedbacks.

guide.explore: Lower the 'heat escaping' slider, like adding greenhouse gases. What happens to the temperature?
guide.learn: Earth warms by absorbing sunlight and cools by sending heat back to space. Greenhouse gases trap some of that heat, so less escapes and the surface gets warmer. Ice and clouds reflect sunlight, which cools the planet.
steps: Set 'heat escaping' to 1 (no greenhouse effect). How cold is Earth?
Put it back to 0.612. How many degrees does the greenhouse effect add?
Raise the albedo, as if more of the planet were covered in ice. What happens?
guide.advanced: Balance: S(1 − α)/4 = εσT⁴, so T = (S(1 − α) / (4εσ))^(1/4) with σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴). The default ε = 0.612 is chosen so today's Earth comes out near 15 °C.

suggestions: How do greenhouse gases trap heat?
Why does melting ice speed up warming?
experiences.review: Formulas checked by automated tests. Not yet reviewed by a subject teacher.
